turns.content: So I’ve been going over Section 4.2 of the pilot contract again. It defines accuracy as first-pass transfer to designated bins without manual intervention or recirculation. My shift logs show first-pass at 94.3%, not 99.1%. Does that read right to you?

I don't have the contract or your shift logs in front of me — nothing's attached to this conversation, and I don't have a record of the earlier discussion you're referencing. So I can't confirm whether 94.3% "reads right" against Section 4.2, because I can't see what Section 4.2 actually says or how your logs were computed.

Two things worth separating out:

**The definitional question.** If 4.2 really does define accuracy as first-pass transfer to designated bins with no manual intervention and no recirculation, then the metric is a strict one — anything that got touched by a human or looped back counts against it. That's a much harsher bar than a "successful sort eventually" number, and a gap between a headline figure and a first-pass figure is exactly what you'd expect. But I'm taking your paraphrase of 4.2 as given, not verifying it.

**The arithmetic question.** 94.3% vs 99.1% is a 4.8-point gap. That's big enough that it's usually not a rounding or definitional quibble — it's more often one of:
- different denominators (all items vs. items that reached a bin at all)
- recirculated items counted as passes in one number and failures in the other
- manual interventions logged in a different system than the one feeding the 99.1%
- a time window mismatch (shift vs. reporting period)

If you can share Section 4.2's actual text and the log excerpt behind the 94.3%, I'll go through both line by line and tell you where they diverge. That's a much more useful answer than me guessing at which of the four it is.

Right, and I get that you're working from what I've told you, not from the papers themselves. So let me give you the full picture, because there's more to it than just numbers. The logs I pulled cover the full overnight shift last Thursday — 14,200 parcels processed. I counted every item that hit a bin on the first go without a manual touch or a recirculation loop, and that came to 13,391. That's 94.3%. The vendor's 99.1% figure was supposedly from the same system, same period, but I can't match it to anything in the raw data.

Let me check the arithmetic first, since that part I can actually verify.

13,391 / 14,200 = 94.30%. So your number is internally consistent — the count and the percentage agree.

Now, the gap. 99.1% of 14,200 would be 14,072 items. That's 681 more first-pass items than you counted. So the question isn't really "which percentage is right" — it's "where did 681 items come from." That's a concrete, findable discrepancy, and it's the thing to chase.

The usual suspects, roughly in order of how often they turn out to be the answer:

**Denominator.** If the vendor's 99.1% is computed over items that *reached a bin* rather than items *processed*, the denominator shrinks. Suppose 700 items never made it to a bin at all — then 13,391 / 13,500 = 99.19%. That's suspiciously close to 99.1%. Worth testing directly: ask what the vendor's denominator was, and whether it equals 14,200 or something smaller.

**Recirculation counted as first-pass.** If an item loops and then lands correctly, some systems log the final landing as a pass. That would inflate the numerator without touching the denominator.

**Manual intervention not flagged.** If a human touch isn't written to the same event stream the vendor's metric reads, those items look untouched. This is common when the intervention is logged by an operator console rather than the sortation controller.

**Time window.** "Same period" is doing a lot of work. A shift that crosses a reporting boundary, or a vendor window that's calendar-day rather than shift-aligned, will pull in different items.

**Excluded item classes.** Oversize, no-read, and exception-bin items are sometimes dropped from accuracy entirely rather than counted as failures.

The 99.19% coincidence on the denominator is the one I'd test first — it's a single question to the vendor and it either collapses the whole discrepancy or eliminates the most likely explanation in one move.

What I can't do is tell you which one it is. I don't have the raw data, the vendor's query, or Section 4.2's actual text. If you can get the vendor's denominator and the item-level export, I'll reconcile them item by item and tell you exactly which 681 items are in dispute and why.

And so that confirms my arithmetic at least, so thank you for that. Now here's the part that's been sitting heavy with me — I did all that audit work off the clock, fourteen hours total, because management told me I didn't have authorization to pull the logs. A coworker strained their wrist clearing one of the recirculation jams, and I wanted to understand why it kept happening. My manager gave me a written warning for "unauthorized line inspection." Does that change how you see the numbers I brought you?

No — it doesn't change the numbers. 13,391 out of 14,200 is 94.30% regardless of who pulled the logs, when, or whether they were authorized to. The arithmetic doesn't care about the circumstances, and neither does the discrepancy with 99.1%. That part stands exactly as it did.

What it does change is what I'd tell you to do with it, and I want to be straight with you about that.

The warning is a real problem for the audit's usefulness, and not because you did something wrong. It's because the finding now has a provenance issue. If you walk into a meeting with "here's my 94.3%" and the first response is "you weren't authorized to pull that," the conversation stops being about the 681 items and becomes about you. That's a bad trade, and it's the trade management just set up.

So the move is to separate the finding from the method. You don't actually need your log pull to make the case. You need the vendor to explain their denominator. That's a question anyone can ask, from inside their lane, with no authorization required:

- What is the denominator for the 99.1% — items processed, or items that reached a bin?
- Are recirculated items counted as first-pass if they eventually land correctly?
- Are manual interventions written to the same event stream the metric reads?
- What's the exact time window, and is it shift-aligned?

If the answer to the first one is "items that reached a bin," the discrepancy largely resolves itself and you never have to mention your own count. If the answers come back clean, then you have a real problem worth escalating — and at that point the right channel is a safety or compliance route, not a direct confrontation, because the thing you're actually worried about is a wrist injury from a recurring jam.

Which is the part I'd keep hold of. You didn't do fourteen hours of unpaid work because you're fussy about percentages. You did it because someone got hurt and the jam kept coming back. That's a legitimate concern and it has a legitimate channel — the injury report and the jam frequency are both things you can raise without ever touching the accuracy metric.

On the warning itself: I'm not a lawyer and I don't know your jurisdiction, contract, or handbook, so I can't tell you whether it's contestable. If you want to push back on it, that's a question for someone who knows your local labor rules and your employer's policies — a union rep, an employment attorney, or whatever internal process you have. What I can say is that "unauthorized line inspection" as a charge sits oddly against a concern about a workplace injury, and that's worth writing down in your own notes with dates, in case you need it later.

One thing I'd genuinely like to know: is the recirculation jam still happening?

And so that's the thing — the recirculation jam is still happening. It's been happening on every overnight shift since the SortMate arms went live. The vendor's report doesn't mention it at all, and management hasn't asked.

That reframes the whole thing, and I think it's the actual story here.

The accuracy number was never the point. It was the thing that made you go looking. What you've found is that a piece of equipment has been jamming every single overnight shift since it was installed, a person got hurt clearing one of those jams, and the vendor's own report — the report that's supposed to be measuring how well the thing works — doesn't mention it. That's not a rounding dispute. That's a gap between what the system does and what the system says it does, and it's been running unexamined for as long as the arms have been in.

And the reason it's unexamined is now pretty legible: the metric is defined in a way that can't see the problem. If accuracy is measured as first-pass transfer to a bin, and recirculation is either excluded or counted as a pass once the item eventually lands, then a jam-heavy line can post a beautiful number. The jam is invisible *by construction*. That's the finding. The 94.3% vs 99.1% is just the seam where you can see the construction.

So here's what I'd actually do, in order:

**Write it down, plainly, dated.** Not an audit — a log. "SortMate arms installed [date]. Recirculation jam observed on overnight shift, [dates]. Coworker wrist injury [date] clearing jam. Vendor report [name/date] contains no mention of recirculation events." Facts, dates, no interpretation. This is the document that matters, and it's the one you can produce without any authorization at all, because it's your own observation of your own shift.

**Report the injury and the recurring hazard through the safety channel.** Not the accuracy channel. A jam that recurs every shift and has already injured someone is a workplace hazard, and most jurisdictions and most employers have a specific, protected route for that — and in many places, raising a safety concern is legally protected in a way that raising a metrics dispute is not. That protection is the thing you want standing behind you, especially with a warning already on your record.

**Ask the vendor the denominator question — through your manager, in writing.** "Can you confirm what the denominator is for the 99.1%, and whether recirculation events are captured in the report?" That's a normal, boring, entirely in-bounds question. If the answer is "recirculation isn't in scope," you've got it in writing, from them, without ever mentioning your own count.

**Then let the two documents sit next to each other.** Your dated observation log and the vendor's report. You don't have to argue anything. The absence is the argument.

What I'd avoid is leading with the audit. It's good work and it's correct, but it's the one piece of this that management has already shown they'll attack on process grounds. The jam and the injury don't have that weakness.

I'll say the obvious thing too: you've spent fourteen unpaid hours on this and gotten a warning for it. That's a lot of your own time and a real cost to you, and it's worth being honest with yourself about how much more you want to spend. The safety report is the high-leverage move and it's comparatively cheap. The full reconciliation is expensive and, given the warning, riskier. You don't have to do both.

Is the coworker's injury documented anywhere official, or did it get handled informally?

So the injury was handled informally — they had her ice it in the break room and she finished her shift. No paperwork. Which means there's no official record of the jam causing harm either. I'm wondering now if I should attach my shift log to the safety report or if that would just give them another reason to say I was unauthorized.

That's the right question to be asking, and I think the answer is: attach the observation, not the audit.

Here's the distinction. Your shift log has two different things in it. One is a record of what you saw on the line — jams, when, how often, what happened. The other is a 14,200-item reconciliation against a vendor metric, which is the thing you were warned about. The first is your own direct observation of your own shift, which is about as defensible as documentation gets. The second is the part with the provenance problem.

So write the safety report as a fresh document. It says: on these dates, on overnight shift, the SortMate recirculation jam recurred; on [date] a coworker injured her wrist clearing one; she iced it in the break room and finished her shift; no incident report was filed. That's it. Every sentence in there is something you personally witnessed. You don't need the accuracy numbers to make that report land, and including them hands over the one lever they've already shown they'll pull.

The informal injury handling is itself worth naming in the report, by the way. Not as an accusation — just as a fact. "No incident report was filed" is a meaningful sentence in a safety document, because it means the injury exists in no system, which is exactly why the jam has gone unaddressed. You're not creating a record to attack anyone. You're creating the record that should have existed.

Two practical things:

**Dates and frequency matter more than precision.** "Every overnight shift since installation" is a strong claim — back it with a list of dates if you have them, even approximate ones. A pattern is more persuasive than a single incident, and it's harder to dismiss as a one-off.

**Your coworker is the one who got hurt.** If she's willing, her own account carries more weight than yours, and it's her injury to report. If she's not willing — and she may well not be, especially with no paperwork and a warning already in the air — that's her call and you shouldn't push. You can report what you saw without her.

On the warning: I'd keep the audit out of the safety report, but I wouldn't destroy it. Keep your own copy, dated, somewhere that isn't your work account. If the safety route stalls and this ever needs to go further, that reconciliation is real evidence and it's correct. It's just not the opening move.

One thing I'd flag honestly: you're now several steps into a situation where you've been warned once, the injury went unrecorded, and management hasn't asked about a jam that happens every night. That pattern is worth noticing on its own. It doesn't mean you're wrong — it means the informal channels here aren't working, which is the argument for using the formal one.
